conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that saw palmetto does not improve BPH symptoms compared to placebo in the longer term, citing Cochrane systematic reviews and the STEP trial to support this negative finding.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Evidence supports "no" — saw palmetto does not meaningfully improve BPH symptoms in the longer term compared with placebo.

**Cochrane review (2012, updated analysis):** The most rigorous evidence comes from the Cochrane systematic review of Serenoa repens for BPH, which pooled 32 randomized controlled trials involving 5,666 men. It concluded that, compared with placebo, Serenoa repens—even at double and triple the usual dose—provided no significant improvement in nocturia, peak urine flow, or urinary symptom scores. A more recent update reaffirmed this, stating "Serenoa repens alone provides little to no benefits for men with lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement" (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001423.pub3/abstract; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10286776/).

**STEP trial (NEJM, 2006):** A well-designed, one-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized 225 men over 49 with moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms to saw palmetto extract (160 mg twice daily) or placebo. The trial found no benefit of saw palmetto over placebo on urinary symptom scores, peak urinary flow, prostate size, quality of life, or other measures after one year of treatment (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085).

**Later confirmation:** Subsequent trials, including one testing higher doses, similarly failed to show benefit over placebo, as summarized in a secondary source reviewing this evidence (https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/321911).

**Conclusion:** The strongest and most consistent evidence—from a large Cochrane meta-analysis and a well-powered year-long RCT—indicates saw palmetto does not improve BPH symptoms compared with placebo in the longer term, confirming the "no" answer.
